claims.text: The target alloy's superconducting transition temperature is primarily governed by competition between electron–phonon coupling and local chemical disorder.
Electron–phonon coupling contributes to superconductivity in high-entropy alloys.
A modest increase in a secondary transition metal elevates the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Increasing the density of states at the Fermi level enhances electron–phonon coupling and pairing interactions.
Local chemical disorder modulates the density of states at the Fermi level.
Increasing the selected transition-metal concentration increases atomic-scale chemical disorder.
A moderate increase in the selected transition metal will systematically raise Tc relative to the baseline.
Beyond an optimal concentration, further addition will cause Tc to plateau or decline.
The starting material is a homogeneous, single-phase five-element solid solution.
A five-element alloy containing approximately 5 atomic percent of each element is near-equiatomic.
The starting material has a known baseline Tc.
The selected secondary transition metal is known to enhance electron–phonon coupling in related HEA systems.
Increasing one element by 1–2 atomic percent while slightly reducing another can preserve both near-equiatomic composition and the single-phase state.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution without extrinsic impurities.
Tc can be compared across the composition series using resistivity and magnetic-susceptibility measurements.
Failure to observe the predicted nonmonotonic modulation of Tc would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: A five-element alloy with approximately 5 atomic percent of each element totals only about 25 atomic percent and therefore cannot itself be a complete near-equiatomic five-element composition.
The intervention says one other element will be reduced to conserve total composition, whereas the experimental design says all four other elements remain fixed while the fifth is increased.

Secondary-phase formation is defined as outside the hypothesis's applicability boundary, but it is also declared to falsify the mechanism. Leaving the stated domain does not by itself test the within-domain mechanistic prediction.
